account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael’s March 2024 product brochure describes a reusable fiber-optic towed decoy, but does not identify an AI model or confirm deployment in this operation. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.

fields.account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael’s March 2024 product brochure describes a reusable fiber-optic towed decoy, but does not identify an AI model or confirm deployment in this operation. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.

fields.account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael’s March 2024 product brochure describes a reusable fiber-optic towed decoy, but does not identify an AI model or confirm deployment in this operation. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.
